Valiantly
VAL-yant-lee
adv.
From valiant, Old French vaillant, from Latin valere, to be strong. Webster 1828: with personal strength or intrepidity; courageously. Scripture uses it only of doing, never of feeling — and always with God named as the one who makes it possible.

Biblical Definition

Valiantly occurs a handful of times in Scripture and the pattern is unvarying: the courage is commanded, the doing is the man’s, and the outcome is God’s. The psalm states it twice, word for word, in two different books: Through God we shall do valiantly: for he it is that shall tread down our enemies (Psalm 60:12; Psalm 108:13). The valour is real and it is through God; the treading down is His alone. Balaam, forced to bless, uses the word of Israel’s future: And Edom shall be a possession, Seir also shall be a possession for his enemies; and Israel shall do valiantly (Numbers 24:18). And Joab, caught between the Syrians before him and the Ammonites behind, gives one of the finest speeches in Scripture and ends it with a submission that is the whole doctrine in a clause: Be of good courage, and let us behave ourselves valiantly for our people, and for the cities of our God: and let the LORD do that which is good in his sight (1 Chronicles 19:13). He will fight as hard as he can, for the right things, and leave the result entirely with God — without knowing in advance whether the result will be victory.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines VALIANTLY as with personal strength and intrepidity; courageously; stoutly; bravely; with the vigour and resolution proper to a valiant man.

expand to see more

VALIANTLY, adv. — With personal strength and intrepidity; courageously; stoutly; bravely.

VALIANT, a. — Brave; courageous; intrepid in danger; heroic.

Performed with valour; as, a valiant act or a valiant defence.

Applied in Scripture to men of war, and to those who behave themselves so for their people and their cities.

From Latin valeo, to be strong — the root also of value, valid, prevail, and convalesce.

Key Scripture

Psalm 60:12 — "Through God we shall do valiantly: for he it is that shall tread down our enemies."

Psalm 108:13 — "Through God we shall do valiantly: for he it is that shall tread down our enemies."

1 Chronicles 19:13 — "Be of good courage, and let us behave ourselves valiantly for our people, and for the cities of our God: and let the LORD do that which is good in his sight."

Numbers 24:18 — "And Edom shall be a possession, Seir also shall be a possession for his enemies; and Israel shall do valiantly."

Modern Corruption

Joab’s formula — fight as hard as you can and leave the outcome with the LORD — is refused by the prosperity teaching that guarantees the outcome in advance and by the fatalism that concludes effort is therefore pointless.

expand to see more

1 Chronicles 19:13 deserves to be memorised. Joab has divided his force, taken the harder half himself, given Abishai a plan for mutual rescue, and then says: Be of good courage, and let us behave ourselves valiantly for our people, and for the cities of our God: and let the LORD do that which is good in his sight. Every element is there. The courage is commanded, not felt into existence. The object is other people and the cities of God, not personal glory. And the outcome is surrendered without a guarantee — he does not say the LORD will give victory, he says let the LORD do what is good. That last clause is the one the prosperity teaching cannot say, because it has promised the result, and it is the one fatalism refuses to earn, because it has declined the fight.

Psalm 60 is worth reading whole for the same reason. It opens with defeat: O God, thou hast cast us off, thou hast scattered us… thou hast made the earth to tremble, and it complains that God goes not out with their armies. Only after that does it reach Through God we shall do valiantly. The confidence is not the absence of the complaint but its resolution, and the psalm places the whole of the valour under the preposition: through God. Numbers 24:18 shows the same doctrine from an unexpected mouth — a hired diviner announcing that Israel shall do valiantly, because God had determined it and no fee could alter the oracle.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chayil (H2428), strength, force, an army, valour; chazaq (H2388), to be strong; Greek andrizomai (G407), to act like a man, to be courageous; krataios (G2900), mighty.

expand to see more

Hebrew chayil (H2428) — strength, valour, an army, and also wealth; we shall do valiantly (Psalm 60:12).

Hebrew chazaq (H2388) — to be strong, to strengthen oneself; be of good courage (1 Chronicles 19:13).

Hebrew gibbor chayil — a mighty man of valour; the standing title for Israel’s warriors, and of Gideon before he had done anything.

Greek andrizomai (G407) — to play the man, to be courageous; quit you like men, be strong (1 Corinthians 16:13).

Greek tharreo (G2292) — to be of good courage, to be confident (2 Corinthians 5:6).

Usage

"Through God we shall do valiantly (Psalm 60:12) — the valour real, and under a preposition."

"Let us behave ourselves valiantly… and let the LORD do that which is good in his sight (1 Chronicles 19:13) — the whole doctrine in one sentence."

"Israel shall do valiantly (Numbers 24:18) — announced by a diviner who was paid to say the opposite."
